title_en: Futures and Options, Explained With One Story
excerpt_en: If you knew the stock market was about to soar, what should you buy to make the most money? Not stocks. Not funds. Options. Here's the whole thing explained with a story about three friends buying houses.
body_en:
If you knew in advance that the stock market was about to soar, what should you buy to make the most money? Stocks? Funds? Wrong on both counts. The answer is options.

Why? Let me tell you a story about buying houses. Once you hear it, you'll understand spot, futures, and options for good.

Three people, one million yuan each

Xiao Zhang, Xiao Li, and you each have one million yuan in cash. All three of you are convinced house prices will surge next year, so you team up and head to City A to speculate on property, where you meet the sales manager, Old Wang.

Old Wang says: we have finished homes ready to move into, and off-plan homes delivered a year from now. One million yuan each. The finished homes require full payment; the off-plan ones can be bought in installments.

Xiao Zhang: spot — cash on the barrelhead

Xiao Zhang glances at his million and says: who are you looking down on? Full payment, of course. He hands over one million yuan, and Old Wang hands him a finished home on the spot.

Money in one hand, goods in the other, settled on the spot — that is a spot transaction.

Swap the house for gold or oil and you get spot gold and spot oil; swap it for stocks and you get spot stocks. Here's a secret: when we trade stocks day to day, what we are actually buying and selling is spot stocks.

Xiao Li: futures — price it today, trade it later

Xiao Li asks: how do the off-plan homes sell? Old Wang says: 200,000 down, and the remaining 800,000 when the home is finished a year from now — cash for keys, then.

Xiao Li thinks it over: I'll take five. So he pays one million in deposits and signs five purchase contracts with Old Wang, agreeing to pay the remaining four million in a year, when Old Wang hands over five homes.

Price it today, trade it in the future, and neither side is allowed to back out — that is a futures contract. The 200,000 deposit per home is called margin. The signed contracts are futures contracts. The number of homes is the position. Paying the balance and taking delivery a year later is physical settlement.

You: options — paying for a right

You pull Old Wang aside: one million a home is a great price, and I want in — but I need some time to think. Is there any way to lock in this price for a year?

Old Wang thinks: actually, yes — our VIP membership card. Buy a card and you can enjoy the one-million member price for a full year. 200,000 per card, one home per card.

You grit your teeth: I'll take five. You hand over one million yuan and get five membership cards. Old Wang promises: for the next year, no matter how high prices climb, you have the right to buy a home at the one-million member price with your card. And of course, if prices fall, you can simply not buy.

Paying money for the right to buy something later at a fixed price — that is an option. The 200,000 per card is the premium. The VIP card itself is the option contract.

Month one: prices rise to 1.2 million

A month later, prices rise to 1.2 million per home. The three of you get together to review:

  • Xiao Zhang: one home in hand, 200,000 profit.
  • Xiao Li: five homes, one million profit.
  • You: five cards — buying five homes and selling them would make a million, but the cards themselves cost a million, so after all that trouble you made exactly nothing.

Everyone gives Xiao Li a thumbs-up: futures are the fierce one — when prices rise, the gains multiply.

Month two: prices fall back to one million

In the second month, prices turn and fall back to one million per home.

  • Xiao Zhang: no gain, no loss.
  • Xiao Li: no gain, no loss.
  • You: the five cards are now useless — market price and member price are identical, so the million in membership fees is down the drain. A net loss of one million.

Compared with you, Xiao Zhang and Xiao Li suddenly feel much better: options don't work, huh — you lose money even when the market goes sideways.

Month three: prices fall to 700,000, and Xiao Li gets liquidated

In the third month, prices keep falling, down to 700,000 per home.

  • Xiao Zhang: one home, 300,000 loss.
  • Xiao Li: five homes, 1.5 million loss.
  • You: homes are now cheaper than the member price, the five cards are worthless, a net loss of one million.

You and Xiao Li look gravely at Xiao Zhang: spot really is the steady one — it holds up best in a bear market. Xiao Zhang comforts you: just a technical correction, don't lose heart, prices will come back.

Just then, Xiao Li gets a call from Old Wang: Mr. Li, you still owe us four million in final payments. Your five homes are now worth only 3.5 million — even selling them all wouldn't cover the four million. The company is worried you'll default, so we need you to top up your margin by 520,000.

Xiao Li is stunned: I don't have the money right now — can't I pay you once prices recover? Old Wang says no: if you can't top up today, the rules say we take back your homes at market price to stop the losses.

He hangs up. And just like that, all five of Xiao Li's homes are repossessed at 700,000 each. Now Xiao Li has no homes — and still owes Old Wang 500,000.

This mechanism — a futures position falling through its margin and being forcibly sold off to stop the losses — is called forced liquidation. In plain terms: getting wiped out. Once liquidated, the contract is terminated immediately and Xiao Li is out of the game. Even if prices bounce back later, it has nothing to do with him anymore.

Old Wang: the short seller, rooting for a fall

Now look at Old Wang: three months ago he sold the homes to Xiao Li for five million, and now he has bought them all back for 3.5 million — making 1.5 million without lifting a finger.

Selling high first and buying low later — that money-making move in reverse is called short selling. Because Old Wang makes money from shorting, he wants prices to fall, so he is a futures short. Xiao Li, meanwhile, wants prices to rise and make money going long, so he is a futures long.

Same logic for your five cards: you are the options long, Old Wang is the options short. Longs and shorts — you win, I lose; I win, you lose. It is a zero-sum game.

A year later: prices hit two million, and your cards pay off

Prices stumbled along and finally, a year later, reached two million per home. Xiao Zhang's finished home nets him a million in profit.

And you are even happier: each card now represents a million in price difference, minus the 200,000 cost, so each card nets 800,000 — five cards, four million.

You rush to the sales office to cash in — and suddenly realize a serious problem: to actually make the profit, you need five million in cash to buy five homes at the member price, then sell them all at the two-million market price. But you spent your entire million on the cards, so you don't have a cent, and the cards are about to expire. Where do you find five million on short notice?

You think hard and finally come up with a plan: you prepare a prop gold bar, find Old Wang, and say: I have five membership cards, I want to exercise them — five homes at the one-million member price. Old Wang says no problem, please pay five million in cash. You calmly pull the fake gold bar from your pocket and hand it over: here is five million in cash. Old Wang takes the plastic-looking bar, pauses — then immediately plays along: fine, no problem, five million received. Then he pulls out five keys: here are the keys to your five off-plan homes, please take them.

You take the five keys and hand them straight back: homes received — and now I'm selling these five homes back to you. Old Wang smiles knowingly: no problem, the market price is two million per home now, five homes is ten million. Your five-million gold bar back, and here is the remaining five million in cash.

Xiao Zhang and Xiao Li stare in disbelief: that works? Is Old Wang really that easy to fool?

After pocketing the cash, you can't resist teasing Old Wang: Mr. Wang, if I'm not mistaken, our off-plan homes haven't even broken ground yet, have they? Old Wang smiles awkwardly: to be honest, that's right. How did you know? You burst out laughing: I guessed it back in month three, when you rushed to repossess Xiao Li's off-plan homes to cash out. But I get it — everyone is here to speculate on the price difference. Whether the homes are built or not doesn't really matter.

All four of you smile knowingly and shake hands: a bet's a bet.

Reality works the same way: nobody ever cared about the goods, only the difference

Sales offices are like this, and exchanges even more so. In reality, there is no gold in a gold futures exchange, and no oil in an oil options exchange. Over 95% of futures and options contracts are ultimately settled in cash — we call it cash settlement — while the share of contracts that end in actual physical delivery is minuscule.

Because most people, just like the four of you, never cared about the goods from start to finish. Only the price difference.

Back to the first question: why options?

Now that you understand spot, futures, and options, back to the first question: why options?

  • Spot stocks are the steadiest: small gains, small losses.
  • Stock futures are the fiercest: 5x leverage, huge swings — but with liquidation risk in the middle.
  • Stock options are the strongest: the premium is a fixed cost, so losses have a floor — but the conditions for profit are also the harshest. Once you correctly call a big move, the payoff is the most dramatic.

Take Nancy Pelosi, who visited Taiwan a few years ago. She has a nickname: the Stock God of Capitol Hill. As Speaker of the House, her signature move was quietly buying large amounts of call options on related industries just before Congress announced major legislation — as if she could see the future. During her tenure, her investment returns far outpaced Warren Buffett's.

See? The Speaker has already shown us with her own actions: if you can truly predict a big move, options are the best tool for the job.

Got it?

This is educational content only, not investment advice.
